$description: Interaction and information-architecture rules (FEAT-008, ADR-025). Each rule is in the SDK's own words and cites its sources (CONTRACT-005). Generated into @ux-builder/ui/catalogue.json by tools/gen-catalogue.mjs; checked by tools/check-rules.mjs.

rules.title: The blueprint follows its contract
rules.statement: A blueprint has the fields CONTRACT-005 requires, no unknown fields, unique screen IDs, and destinations that name existing screens.
rules.rationale: Every other check reads the blueprint; a malformed one would make their findings meaningless.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-005: blueprint

rules.title: Screens are built from catalogue patterns
rules.statement: Every screen names a pattern the installed SDK ships.
rules.rationale: A screen from a pattern inherits its layout, states and adaptation; an invented one inherits none of them.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-005: blueprint

rules.title: A phone-width bar holds at most five destinations
rules.statement: In an app that supports the compact size class, keep the top-level destinations to five; group the rest or move them to a drawer.
rules.rationale: A bottom bar or tab bar has room for only a few equal targets; more makes each too small to read and tap.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Apple HIG: Tab bars

rules.title: Navigation stays visible on wide screens
rules.statement: From the expanded size class, show primary navigation as a standing rail or side navigation, not behind a menu button.
rules.rationale: Wide windows have room for it, and hiding destinations makes people hunt for them.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Android Developers: Design for large screens

rules.title: Destinations are links; menus are for actions
rules.statement: Move between top-level destinations with navigation links; keep menu buttons for actions on the current page or item.
rules.rationale: People expect navigation to be visible, bookmarkable and announced as navigation; a menu hides it and changes its semantics.

sources.title: WAI-ARIA APG: Landmark regions

rules.title: Show one pane until there is room for two
rules.statement: Use one pane in compact and medium windows, two from expanded (a list beside its detail), and three only in extra-large ones.
rules.rationale: Splitting a narrow window makes both panes cramped; a wide one wastes space with a single pane.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints
Material 3: Canonical layout examples
Android Developers: Design for large screens

rules.title: Keep dense content in one pane at medium
rules.statement: At the medium size class, use two panes only for sparse content with clear actions, such as settings; keep dense lists and tables in one.
rules.rationale: Two dense panes in a tablet-width window reduce usability.

sources.title: Material 3: Breakpoints

rules.title: Use a modal only when it clearly helps
rules.statement: Present a task modally only when it needs focus or a decision before the person continues; otherwise keep it in the page.
rules.rationale: A modal takes people out of their context and must be dismissed before they can return.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: One modal at a time
rules.statement: Never open a modal on top of another, and never show more than one alert at once; close one before presenting the next.
rules.rationale: Stacked modals add clutter and make people lose track of the context they came from.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: A modal names its task
rules.statement: Give every modal a title that says what the task is, as its accessible name.
rules.rationale: People who enter a modal may not return to it straight away; the title keeps their place, and assistive technology announces it.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: A modal can always be dismissed
rules.statement: Give every modal an obvious way out (Cancel, Close or Done), and let Escape close it.
rules.rationale: A modal that is hard to leave traps people; keyboard users rely on Escape.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality
WAI-ARIA APG: Dialog (Modal) pattern

rules.title: Ask before discarding someone's work
rules.statement: When closing a modal would lose what the person entered, explain that and let them save, discard or keep editing.
rules.rationale: Losing typed work to a stray tap or swipe is a failure people remember.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: Keep modal tasks short, with one path
rules.statement: Keep a modal task brief; if it needs several steps, give them a single path and no buttons that could be mistaken for dismissing it.
rules.rationale: A long or branching task inside a modal feels like an app within the app and makes people forget how they got there.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: Destructive actions are safeguarded
rules.statement: Give every destructive action a safeguard: Undo when the loss is expected and reversible, a confirmation only when it is unexpected or irreversible; never neither, and not both.
rules.rationale: Warning about expected deletions trains people to dismiss warnings; no safeguard at all loses data.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback
WCAG 2.2: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)

rules.title: Show status where it belongs
rules.statement: Show the status of something next to it, passively; interrupt with an alert only for critical, actionable information.
rules.rationale: Interruptions lose their effect when they are used for unimportant news.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback

rules.title: Say why a command cannot run
rules.statement: When an action cannot be carried out, say why and what to do, in text next to it.
rules.rationale: A control that silently does nothing looks broken.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Feedback

rules.title: Show something while content loads
rules.statement: Show placeholder content, such as a skeleton, as soon as a region starts loading; never leave it blank.
rules.rationale: An empty region reads as a broken app.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading

rules.title: Match the progress indicator to what is known
rules.statement: Use a determinate progress indicator when the duration is known and an indeterminate one when it is not.
rules.rationale: A bar that moves honestly helps people decide whether to wait.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading

rules.title: Screens of data handle empty, loading and error
rules.statement: A screen that shows a collection, a record or figures declares its empty, loading and error states.
rules.rationale: These states are where most data screens fail; a pattern supports them only when the screen supplies them.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Loading
Apple HIG: Feedback

rules.title: One primary action per page or dialog
rules.statement: Give each page region or dialog at most one primary (filled) button; make the others secondary or text buttons.
rules.rationale: When everything is emphasised, nothing is, and people hesitate over which action is the main one.

sources.title: Material 3: Buttons
Apple HIG: Buttons

rules.title: Touch targets are finger-sized
rules.statement: Under touch input, make every control at least the theme's touch-target size (44 points on Apple platforms, 48 dp in Material).
rules.rationale: Small targets cause mis-taps, especially for people with limited dexterity.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Layout
Material 3: States
WCAG 2.2: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)

rules.title: Nothing is reachable only by hovering
rules.statement: Under touch input, never put content or actions where only hovering reveals them.
rules.rationale: Touch screens have no hover; what hover reveals is unreachable.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.4.13 Content on Hover or Focus
Material 3: States

rules.title: Keyboard focus is always visible
rules.statement: Show a visible focus indicator on every focusable control, distinct from hover and selection.
rules.rationale: Keyboard users need to see where they are; state is shown in more than one way so it does not rely on colour alone.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 2.4.7 Focus Visible
Material 3: States

rules.title: Keep lines of prose readable
rules.statement: Keep running text to at most 80 characters per line, 40 to 60 where possible, by limiting the measure rather than shrinking the type.
rules.rationale: Long lines make it hard to find the start of the next one.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.4.8 Visual Presentation
Material 3: Breakpoints

rules.title: An embedded view has no shell of its own
rules.statement: An embedded view draws no app shell, primary navigation or brand; the host provides its chrome, title and pins.
rules.rationale: Two sets of chrome nested inside each other confuse people and waste a small panel.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-012 and ADR-024: embedded views

rules.title: An embedded view works in a narrow panel
rules.statement: An embedded view supports the compact and medium size classes, since a host's panel is often that narrow even on a desktop.
rules.rationale: Hosts place views in side panels and inline frames, not full windows.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-012 and ADR-024: embedded views
Material 3: Breakpoints

rules.title: An embedded view does one task
rules.statement: Keep an embedded view to one screen and one task; put further steps in modal tasks or sections of that screen.
rules.rationale: A view is reached from one tool call; a second level of navigation inside it has nowhere to live in the host.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-012 and ADR-024: embedded views
Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: An embedded view declares its states
rules.statement: Every screen of an embedded view, whatever its pattern, declares its empty, loading and error states.
rules.rationale: A view is opened by a tool call that may return nothing, still be running or fail; the host has no page of its own to show for any of them.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-012 and ADR-024: embedded views
Apple HIG: Loading

rules.title: An embedded view wears the host's theme
rules.statement: Take the theme only from the host's styles and appearance, and follow the host when it changes them.
rules.rationale: A view that brings its own theme stands out from every other view in the host.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-012 and ADR-024: embedded views

rules.title: AI-made content is labelled
rules.statement: Content made by AI is labelled as AI-made where it appears, or sits in a region whose label says so.
rules.rationale: People judge and check content differently when they know a model wrote it; an unlabelled answer borrows trust it has not earned.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (transparency)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G1)
Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (core principles)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (explainability and trust)

rules.title: The AI is not presented as a person
rules.statement: The UI never presents the AI as a person: no first-person thinking or feeling, and no human name or face that implies a human author.
rules.rationale: Human cues make people over-trust a model and misjudge what it can do or who is accountable for its output.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (transparency)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (differentiated from humans)

rules.title: Say what the AI can and cannot do
rules.statement: At first use, the screen says what the AI can and cannot do, and that its results may need checking.
rules.rationale: A correct mental model at the start prevents both over-reliance and abandonment after the first wrong answer.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G1, G2)
Apple HIG: Generative AI (set clear expectations)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (mental models)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (first run)

rules.title: Offer starting points
rules.statement: An open-ended prompt offers suggested starting points, and they are never the only way to start.
rules.rationale: A blank prompt gives no clue what to ask; suggestions teach the scope without boxing the user in.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (curated suggestions)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (example prompts)
ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (CONV-05)

rules.title: The task works without the AI
rules.statement: Where AI adds to a task rather than being the task, the task can still be done without it.
rules.rationale: Models fail, are unavailable, or are declined by the user; an add-on must not take the underlying job hostage.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (non-AI fallback)

rules.title: Generation can be stopped
rules.statement: While AI is generating or working, a Stop control is reachable and named; stopping keeps what has arrived and says that it stopped.
rules.rationale: A wrong or runaway answer wastes time and can do harm; the user needs to end it at once without losing what is useful.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (intervention during execution)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G9)
ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (CONV-03)

rules.title: Output can be corrected
rules.statement: AI output can be edited, retried, regenerated or reverted, and the screen says when a correction has taken effect.
rules.rationale: Model output is often nearly right; fixing it must be cheaper than starting again, and the user must see that the fix landed.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (refine or revert; acknowledge corrections)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G9)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (correction pathways)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (feedback and control)

rules.title: Suggestions can be dismissed
rules.statement: An AI suggestion the user did not ask for can be dismissed in one action, and stays dismissed.
rules.rationale: Unrequested suggestions that cannot be put away, or that come back, turn help into noise.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G8)
Apple HIG: Generative AI (dismiss unwanted content)

rules.title: The agent can be turned off, and shows its state
rules.statement: The user can turn the agent off, and its state (off, idle, working, waiting for you) is shown.
rules.rationale: People need to know whether something is acting for them, and to stop it entirely when they choose.

sources.title: Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (core principles: on, off and status)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G17)

rules.title: List the agent's high-impact actions
rules.statement: A screen whose agent acts lists the actions it can take that are irreversible, costly or seen by other people.
rules.rationale: Only actions that are named can be given an approval; an undeclared payment or message is approved by nobody.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (high-impact scenarios)
Apple HIG: Generative AI (confirm significant actions)

rules.title: High-impact actions wait for approval
rules.statement: Each high-impact action waits for the user's approval, shows what will happen and to what, offers Deny, and is never approved on the user's behalf.
rules.rationale: An agent that pays, sends or deletes on its own reading of a request can do damage that no undo repairs.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (confirm significant actions)
Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (permission to proceed)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G16)
ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (AGT-T-04)

rules.title: The plan and next step are shown
rules.statement: When an agent works in steps, its plan and next step are shown, each step with its status, and a change of plan is shown too.
rules.rationale: A visible plan lets the user catch a wrong direction before it is acted on, and know where the agent is.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (presentation of plan; preview of next steps)

rules.title: A working agent can be interrupted
rules.statement: A working agent can be paused or stopped at any step, and the user can then give a new instruction.
rules.rationale: Users often see a mistake mid-run; they need to steer then, not after the agent finishes.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (intervention; interrupting then following up)
Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (control)

rules.title: Say who is acting
rules.statement: When the user can take over and hand back, the screen states who is acting now, and the agent's actions are distinguishable from the user's.
rules.rationale: Two actors on one UI collide unless each knows who has control and which changes the other made.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (UI context; takeover cues; distinct agent visuals)

rules.title: Failed steps can be recovered
rules.statement: A failed step is described at that step and in text, and the user can retry it or return to an earlier step without starting over.
rules.rationale: Restarting a long run for one failed step wastes the work done and discourages using the agent at all.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (agent errors; reverting to a prior step)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (avoid forcing restarts)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G9)

rules.title: A finished run is summarised
rules.statement: A finished run ends with a summary of what was done, with the detail available on request.
rules.rationale: The user must be able to check what an agent did on their behalf without replaying every step.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (concise summary; progressive disclosure)

rules.title: Status reaches a user who is not watching
rules.statement: Progress, duration and step status reach a user who is not watching (a persistent status region or a notification), above all for risky steps.
rules.rationale: People hand work to agents so they can look away; status shown only in a transient view is missed.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (users rarely monitor)
Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (nudging more than notifying)

rules.title: Show what the output relies on
rules.statement: Output that relies on documents, data or the web shows which, linked where possible.
rules.rationale: Sources let the user check an answer and judge how far to trust it.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G11)
Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (surface contextual signals)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (explainability and trust)
ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (AGT-T-03)

rules.title: State uncertainty and assumptions
rules.statement: The UI says when the AI is unsure or has assumed something the user did not say, instead of presenting a guess as fact.
rules.rationale: Confident presentation of a guess leads people to act on it; stated uncertainty sets appropriate trust.

sources.title: Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (embrace uncertainty; appropriate trust)
Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (seamfulness; ambiguity)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G2)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (explainability and trust)

rules.title: Clarify ambiguous high-stakes requests
rules.statement: In a high-stakes step an ambiguous request is clarified with the user; in a low-stakes one a stated default may be used.
rules.rationale: Guessing is cheap when a wrong guess is cheap; on a costly step a question is cheaper than a mistake.

sources.title: Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (ambiguity)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G10)

rules.title: Help the user ask differently
rules.statement: A blocked or unhelpful result says why, where it can, and how to ask differently.
rules.rationale: Without a hint, people repeat the same request or give up; a reason and a suggestion turn a dead end into a retry.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (help people improve requests)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (errors and graceful failure)

rules.title: Ask before data leaves the device
rules.statement: Before personal data or usage leaves the device for an AI feature, the user is told what is sent and why, gives permission, and can opt out later.
rules.rationale: People cannot weigh a feature's benefit against a privacy cost they were never told about.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (privacy)

rules.title: Feedback on output is optional and specific
rules.statement: Users can give feedback on a specific output; giving it is optional and never blocks the task.
rules.rationale: Specific feedback improves the system; compulsory feedback interrupts the work it is meant to improve.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (continuous improvement)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G15)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (feedback and control)

rules.title: What the AI remembers is visible
rules.statement: What the AI remembers or has learned about the user can be seen and changed.
rules.rationale: Hidden memory surprises people and makes wrong assumptions impossible to correct.

sources.title: Microsoft Design: UX design for agents (the past; transparency of knowledge)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G12, G13)

rules.title: Tell users when the AI changes
rules.statement: When the AI's behaviour or model changes in a way users would notice, they are told.
rules.rationale: A silent change breaks the habits and trust people built on the old behaviour.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G14, G18)
Apple HIG: Generative AI (test model updates)

rules.title: Do not infer or stereotype people
rules.statement: The AI does not infer personal or cultural attributes it can ask for, and is tested with diverse people for stereotyped output.
rules.rationale: Inferred attributes are often wrong and can offend; stereotyped output excludes the people it misrepresents.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (inclusion)
Microsoft HAX Toolkit: Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction (G6)
Google PAIR: People + AI Guidebook (fairness)

rules.title: Inline UI comes from renderable components
rules.statement: An assistant renders inline only components the catalogue marks renderable.
rules.rationale: Renderable components have validated props and work inside a message; anything else may break the conversation or carry unsafe markup.

sources.title: ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (GEN-01)
ux-builder ADR-023: generative UI libraries are bridged

rules.title: Pre-filled values are the user's to submit
rules.statement: Values the AI pre-fills in an inline form or wizard are editable, and are submitted only by the user's own action.
rules.rationale: A form filled and sent by the model is an action taken without consent, however helpful the values.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (keep people in control)
Cheng, Liang, Schoop and Nichols: Mapping the Design Space of User Experience for Computer Use Agents (IUI '26) (permission to proceed)

rules.title: Regeneration keeps what the user typed
rules.statement: Regenerating an answer never silently discards what the user typed into its inline UI.
rules.rationale: Losing typed input to a regenerate click punishes the user for asking for a better answer.

sources.title: Apple HIG: Generative AI (refine without losing work)
ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (GEN-04)

rules.title: Submitted inline UI stays readable
rules.statement: A submitted inline component stays readable in the conversation, shows what was submitted, and can no longer be changed.
rules.rationale: The history is the record of what the user agreed to; it must not be editable or disappear.

sources.title: ux-builder FEAT-007: generative UI (AGT-T-04, GEN-04)

rules.title: AI screens declare their role
rules.statement: A screen that shows AI content declares its AI role in the blueprint.
rules.rationale: The AI rules apply by declared role; an undeclared AI screen escapes every rule meant for it.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-028: AI experience rules apply by declared role and marked markup

rules.title: The user starts the action
rules.statement: Labels keep the user as the one who starts an action ("Summarize", "Summarize with Assistant"), not the AI ("Assistant, summarize").
rules.rationale: Labels that make the AI the actor blur who is responsible and read as the AI acting on its own.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Human-centered design for agents (built for intent)
ux-builder ADR-028: AI experience rules apply by declared role and marked markup

rules.title: A card has few primary actions
rules.statement: A card offers few primary actions, usually one to three and never more than six.
rules.rationale: Many actions crowd a small card and make the main next step hard to find.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (anatomy; actions)
Adaptive Cards documentation: design best practices

rules.title: Card text wraps
rules.statement: Text blocks and choice labels in a card wrap, so text is never cut off on a narrow screen.
rules.rationale: Cards are shown in narrow chat columns and phones, where unwrapped text is truncated.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (text)
Adaptive Cards documentation: design best practices

rules.title: Every card input has a label
rules.statement: Every input in a card has a label of its own; a placeholder is never the only label.
rules.rationale: A placeholder disappears as the user types and is not reliably read by assistive technology.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (label property)

rules.title: Validated card inputs explain errors
rules.statement: An input in a card that validates (required, pattern, range) says what is wrong in an error message.
rules.rationale: Without a message, the user sees only that submission failed, not what to fix.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (error messages)

rules.title: A card's title is a heading
rules.statement: A card with more than its title marks the title as a heading.
rules.rationale: Screen-reader users navigate by headings; an unmarked title hides the card's structure.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (heading style)
Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (anatomy: header)

rules.title: A card uses few columns
rules.statement: A column layout in a card uses few columns (at most three) and no fixed widths wider than a compact screen allows.
rules.rationale: Columns squeeze content on narrow hosts until it is unreadable or overflows.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (column layouts)

rules.title: A card is laid out narrow first
rules.statement: A card is laid out for the narrowest width it will show at and still works wider; it never scrolls sideways.
rules.rationale: The same card appears in a phone, a side panel and a wide window; designing for the widest breaks the others.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (best practices)

rules.title: Reading order matches visual order
rules.statement: The order a card is read and tabbed in matches the order it is seen in.
rules.rationale: A mismatch confuses keyboard and screen-reader users, who meet the content in a different order from everyone else.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (logical tab order)

rules.title: Card images have alternative text
rules.statement: Every informative image in a card has alternative text.
rules.rationale: Without it, people who cannot see the image lose what it says.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.1.1 Non-text Content
Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (alternative text)

rules.title: Card images suit light and dark themes
rules.statement: Images in a card use transparent backgrounds so they suit light and dark themes, and text never sits on a colour that hurts reading.
rules.rationale: The host chooses the theme; an image with a baked-in background clashes with one of them.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (images)

rules.title: Card action titles say what they do
rules.statement: Action titles in a card say what they do; never "Click here", or "Submit" alone where the outcome is unclear.
rules.rationale: An action read out of context must still tell the user what will happen.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (descriptive action titles)

rules.title: Card inputs are not hidden
rules.statement: Inputs in a card, above all validated ones, are not hidden behind a toggle; if one must be, the toggle says what it shows.
rules.rationale: A hidden required input blocks submission with an error the user cannot see.

sources.title: Copilot Studio: Accessibility tips for Adaptive Cards (visibility caution)

rules.title: A card declares a supported version
rules.statement: A card declares a schema version the host supports (1.6 or lower) and gives a fallback for anything outside it.
rules.rationale: Hosts differ in what they render; a declared version and a fallback keep a card working across them.

sources.title: Adaptive Cards: Motivations and Principles (interoperability)
ux-builder ADR-029: Adaptive Cards render with SDK components in the app's theme

rules.title: Cards are sent sparingly
rules.statement: An agent sends a card only when it helps; cards that scroll out of view lose their use.
rules.rationale: A conversation full of cards buries the ones that matter and the actions on them.

sources.title: Microsoft Teams: Designing Adaptive Cards (frequency)

rules.title: High-impact card actions are marked
rules.statement: A card action that pays, sends, deletes or publishes is marked high-impact, so the host asks for approval.
rules.rationale: The host can ask for approval only for actions it knows are high-impact.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-029: Adaptive Cards render with SDK components in the app's theme
Apple HIG: Generative AI (confirm significant actions)

rules.title: Every screen can be reached
rules.statement: Every screen is reached from a destination (or, in a view, its first screen) through actions, at every size class the app supports; leaving by external counts as a way on.
rules.rationale: A screen no one can reach is dead code at best, and at worst the only place a task can be done.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint

rules.title: No screen or modal is a dead end
rules.statement: A screen or modal that declares actions offers a way on or back: another screen, back, external, or a modal's dismiss.
rules.rationale: A user who cannot leave a screen must abandon the app or the task.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint
Apple HIG: Modality

rules.title: Actions lead somewhere that exists
rules.statement: Every action's target names a screen, a modal of its screen, back, a state or external.
rules.rationale: A target that names nothing is a broken link in the plan; every check of the flow depends on targets that exist.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint

rules.title: One primary action, stated once
rules.statement: A screen marks at most one action primary, and when it also gives primaryAction, that is the same action.
rules.rationale: Two answers to which action leads make the screen's emphasis, and the checks of it, ambiguous.

sources.title: ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint

rules.title: A journey can be walked
rules.statement: Each step of a journey names an action its screen has, and the next step is where that action leads; the first step is on the entry, and an alternate starts where it branches.
rules.rationale: A journey that cannot be walked over the flow describes an app that does not exist.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint

rules.title: Risky steps are safeguarded
rules.statement: A journey step that takes a destructive action has its safeguard (undo or confirm), and one that takes a high-impact action has its approval.
rules.rationale: The journey is the path users actually take; a missing safeguard on it is a loss users will meet.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
WCAG 2.2: 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)

rules.title: Journeys cover their error states
rules.statement: A journey through a screen that declares an error state has an alternate that covers that state.
rules.rationale: The error path is where users most need a planned way to recover, and is the one most often left unplanned.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint
Apple HIG: Feedback

rules.title: Journeys follow the HELIX stories
rules.statement: With a HELIX marker, every story a screen serves has a journey, and each journey's story and criteria exist in HELIX; the stories are read, never written.
rules.rationale: HELIX governs and the blueprint projects it; a story with no journey, or a criterion HELIX lacks, is drift between them.

sources.title: ux-builder ADR-030: the blueprint holds screen flows and journeys
ux-builder FEAT-012: screen flows and user journeys in the blueprint

rules.title: A journey grows only by decision
rules.statement: When a change adds a screen, a step, a required input or a decision to a journey, a recorded decision names the addition and answers why it is needed and what simpler option was considered.
rules.rationale: Each added step or input raises the interaction cost of the task; making the cost visible and deliberate keeps an app from growing more complicated one reasonable change at a time.

sources.title: Nielsen Norman Group: Interaction Cost
ux-builder FEAT-018: guided design loop (GDL-11, GDL-12)

rules.title: The theme is applied
rules.statement: The page loads the declared theme's CSS and the theme's tokens resolve on the themed element.
rules.rationale: Every other theme rule measures against the theme's tokens; without them the app wears no theme at all.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-003: theme selection
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Colours come from the theme's tokens
rules.statement: Every colour the app draws is one of the theme's colour tokens, or a mix of two of them.
rules.rationale: A hard-coded colour does not follow the theme, its appearances or its contrast checks.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-001: token names
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Text uses the theme's fonts
rules.statement: Text is set in the font families the theme names, through its type tokens.
rules.rationale: A foreign font breaks the theme's voice and its measured line lengths.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-001: token names
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Corners use the theme's radii
rules.statement: Rounded corners use the theme's radius tokens.
rules.rationale: Radii are part of a design system's shape language; ad hoc values make the app look assembled from parts.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-001: token names
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: The app does not redefine theme tokens
rules.statement: The app never sets --piq-* tokens itself; only the theme defines them.
rules.rationale: An override silently forks the theme, so a theme change or a new appearance no longer reaches that part of the app.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-001: token names
ux-builder CONTRACT-003: theme selection

rules.title: The app does not restyle SDK widgets
rules.statement: The app does not restyle the SDK's widgets with its own CSS; it chooses variants and tokens instead.
rules.rationale: Restyled widgets drift from the design system and lose the states, focus rings and contrast the SDK guarantees.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Icons, logo, loaders and controls come from the SDK
rules.statement: Icons, the logo, loading indicators and controls are the SDK's components, not drawn by the app.
rules.rationale: The SDK's components carry the theme, accessible names and states; hand-drawn ones carry none of that.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: No other UI library's components
rules.statement: The page renders no component from another UI library.
rules.rationale: A second component library brings its own tokens, focus handling and look, which the theme cannot reach.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Everything visible is inside the themed element
rules.statement: Every visible element sits inside the element the theme is applied to.
rules.rationale: Content outside the themed element gets browser defaults instead of the theme.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-003: theme selection
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: The favicon and logo follow the theme
rules.statement: The page's favicon and logo are the theme's brand assets.
rules.rationale: A brand that does not match the theme tells users they may be in the wrong place.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-002: brand and design-system files
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: The theme's fonts are loaded from the SDK
rules.statement: The theme's fonts are loaded, from the SDK's font files.
rules.rationale: A missing font falls back to a system face with different metrics, which shifts the layout.

sources.title: ux-builder CONTRACT-002: brand and design-system files
ux-builder CONTRACT-004: app integration

rules.title: Text and controls meet contrast minimums
rules.statement: Text meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) and controls' boundaries at least 3:1, in every appearance.
rules.rationale: Low contrast makes text and controls unreadable for people with low vision and in bright light.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)
WCAG 2.2: 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast

rules.title: Content reflows without sideways scrolling
rules.statement: The page does not scroll sideways at the audited width, down to 320 CSS pixels.
rules.rationale: Two-way scrolling makes reading and operating the page very hard on a narrow screen or when zoomed.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 1.4.10 Reflow

rules.title: Pointer targets are large enough
rules.statement: Pointer targets are at least the theme's minimum target size, and never smaller than 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
rules.rationale: Small targets are hard to hit for people with limited dexterity and on touch screens.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)

rules.title: A focused control is never hidden
rules.statement: A control that receives keyboard focus is never entirely hidden behind sticky or fixed content.
rules.rationale: Keyboard users cannot see where they are when the focused control is covered.

sources.title: WCAG 2.2: 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
